question: At what temperature must hot-held TCS food be kept?
answer: Hot-held TCS food must be maintained at 57°C (135°F) or above, except that roasts cooked to a specific time and temperature or reheated may be held at 54°C (130°F) or above [food_code_2022, §3-501.16, p. 93].

answer: Refrigerated, ready-to-eat TCS food prepared and held in a food establishment for more than 24 hours must be clearly marked to be consumed, sold, or discarded within a maximum of 7 days when held at a temperature of 5°C (41°F) or less, with the day of preparation counted as Day 1. [food_code_2022, §3-501.17, pp. 93-94]

question: What are the time limits for cooling cooked food?

question: What temperature must leftovers reach when they are reheated for hot holding, and how quickly?
answer:
Time/temperature control for safety food that is cooked, cooled, and reheated for hot holding shall be reheated so that all parts of the food reach a temperature of at least 74°C (165°F) for 15 seconds [food_code_2022, §3-403.10 to 3-403.11, pp. 89-90]. 

For food reheated in a microwave oven, all parts must reach at least 74°C (165°F), and the food must be rotated or stirred, covered, and allowed to stand covered for 2 minutes after reheating [food_code_2022, §3-403.10 to 3-403.11, pp. 89-90]. Commercially processed, packaged ready-to-eat food from an inspected food processing plant shall be heated to at least 57°C (135°F) [food_code_2022, §3-403.10 to 3-403.11, pp. 89-90]. Reheating for hot holding must be done rapidly, and the time the food is between 5°C (41°F) and the required reheating temperature may not exceed 2 hours [food_code_2022, §3-403.10 to 3-403.11, pp. 89-90].

question: How often do cutting boards and other food-contact surfaces used with TCS food have to be cleaned during the day?

* Each time there is a change from working with raw FOODS to working with READY-TO-EAT FOODS [food_code_2022, §4-602.11, p. 127].

question: How high off the floor must food be stored?
answer:

* Pressurized beverage containers, cased food in waterproof containers (such as bottles or cans), and milk containers in plastic crates may be stored on a clean floor that is not exposed to floor moisture [food_code_2022, §3-305.11, p. 81].

question: What do I have to put on the menu if we serve raw oysters or burgers cooked to order?
answer:
If you serve raw or undercooked animal foods like raw oysters or burgers cooked to order, you must inform consumers of the increased risk of foodborne illness by way of a disclosure and reminder using brochures, deli case or menu advisories, label statements, table tents, placards, or other effective written means [food_code_2022, §3-602.12 to 3-603.11, pp. 103-104].

The disclosure must include a description of the animal-derived foods (such as “oysters on the half shell (raw oysters)” and “hamburgers (can be cooked to order)”) or identification of the animal-derived foods by asterisking them to a footnote that states that the items are served raw or undercooked, or contain (or may contain) raw or undercooked ingredients [food_code_2022, §3-602.12 to 3-603.11, pp. 103-104]. 

The reminder must include asterisking the animal-derived foods requiring disclosure to a footnote that states that consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness (with or without the addition of "especially if you have certain medical conditions"), or that written information regarding the safety of these items is available upon request [food_code_2022, §3-602.12 to 3-603.11, pp. 103-104].
judge_explanation: The assistant accurately explains the requirements for a consumer advisory (disclosure and reminder) using the exact details and terminology from the provided Food Code text.

question: What temperature should refrigerated TCS food be when a delivery arrives?

Additionally, raw eggs must be received in refrigerated equipment that maintains an ambient air temperature of 7°C (45°F) or less, and all received TCS food must be free of evidence of previous temperature abuse [food_code_2022, §3-202.11, pp. 69-70].

question: Where are kitchen staff allowed to eat or drink during their shift?
answer:
Employees may eat, drink, or use tobacco products only in designated areas where contamination of exposed food, clean equipment, utensils, linens, unwrapped single-service and single-use articles, or other protected items cannot result [food_code_2022, §2-401.11, p. 64]. 

As an exception, a food employee may drink from a closed beverage container if the container is handled to prevent contamination of the employee's hands, the container itself, and exposed food, clean equipment, utensils, linens, and unwrapped single-service and single-use articles [food_code_2022, §2-401.11, p. 64].

question: What are the Big 6 foodborne pathogens?
answer:
The "Big 6" foodborne pathogens are a group of highly infectious pathogens that can easily be transmitted by food employees and cause severe illness [employee_health_handbook, p. 3]. They include:

* Norovirus [employee_health_handbook, p. 3]
* Hepatitis A virus [employee_health_handbook, p. 3]
* Salmonella Typhi [employee_health_handbook, p. 3]
* Shigella spp. [employee_health_handbook, p. 3]
* Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli [employee_health_handbook, p. 3]
* Nontyphoidal Salmonella [employee_health_handbook, p. 3]
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly lists all six Big 6 pathogens matching the reference answer and supports every claim with direct evidence from the text.

question: One of our employees has turned yellow in the skin and eyes. What should the manager do?
answer:
Have the food employee stop work immediately [employee_health_handbook, p. 8]. Inquire about how long the employee has been experiencing jaundice [employee_health_handbook, p. 8]. 

If the onset of jaundice occurred within the last 7 calendar days, exclude the employee from the food establishment, unless they provide written medical documentation from a health practitioner specifying that the jaundice is not caused by hepatitis A virus or other fecal-orally transmitted infections [food_code_2022, §2-201.12, pp. 52-53]. Report the case of jaundice to the regulatory authority, and ensure the employee's return to work is approved by the regulatory authority [employee_health_handbook, p. 8].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly identifies all necessary manager actions regarding an employee with jaundice based on the provided evidence.

question: What is the difference between excluding and restricting a food employee?
answer:
Exclusion means a food employee is not permitted to work in or enter a food establishment as a food employee in any areas where food is received, prepared, stored, packaged, served, vended, transported, or purchased [employee_health_handbook, p. 10]. 

Restriction means a food employee’s activities are limited to prevent the risk of transmitting a disease through food, meaning they cannot work with exposed food, clean equipment, utensils, linens, or unwrapped single-service or single-use articles (such as working as a cashier, seating patrons, bussing tables, or performing non-food cleaning or maintenance tasks) [employee_health_handbook, p. 10].
judge_explanation: The assistant accurately explains the definitions and differences of exclusion and restriction, and all claims are fully supported by the provided evidence passages.

question: Can an employee with Crohn's disease keep working if she has diarrhea?
answer: Yes, a food employee can keep working if she has diarrhea, provided she can provide medical documentation indicating that the symptoms are from a non-infectious condition such as Crohn's disease [employee_health_handbook, p. 9].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly states that an employee with diarrhea can continue working if they provide medical documentation that it is due to a non-infectious condition like Crohn's disease, and this is fully supported by the evidence.

question: What should our written plan for cleaning up vomit or diarrhea in the restaurant cover?
answer:
Your written plan for cleaning up vomit or diarrhea events must address specific actions employees must take to minimize contamination and exposure, including:

* **Containment and Removal:** Procedures for containing and removing discharges, including airborne particulates [employee_health_handbook, p. 20], and segregating contaminated areas to minimize unnecessary exposure of employees, customers, and others [employee_health_handbook, p. 20].
* **Cleaning and Disinfection:** Procedures for cleaning, sanitizing, and disinfecting contaminated surfaces [employee_health_handbook, p. 20], as well as the disposal or cleaning and disinfection of tools and equipment used in the response [employee_health_handbook, p. 20].
* **Food Evaluation:** Procedures for evaluating and disposing of any food that may have been exposed to the discharges [employee_health_handbook, p. 20].
* **Supplies and Equipment:** Ensuring the availability and proper use of effective disinfectants (such as EPA-registered products sufficient to inactivate norovirus), personal protective equipment (PPE), and other cleaning equipment [employee_health_handbook, p. 20].
* **Employee Protection and Training:** The circumstances and notification rules for food employees on wearing and using personal protective equipment correctly [employee_health_handbook, p. 20].
* **Disease Transmission & Personnel:** Minimizing disease transmission by excluding or restricting ill employees according to §2-201.12 of the Food Code and promptly removing ill customers from food areas [employee_health_handbook, p. 20].
* **Implementation Conditions:** The specific conditions under which the plan will be implemented [employee_health_handbook, p. 20].
judge_explanation: The assistant provides a thorough and accurate list of all the elements a written plan should cover based on the retrieved evidence, and every point is directly supported.

question: What rules should staff follow when they use single-use gloves?
answer: Staff must always wash hands before donning single-use gloves, and they must never wash or reuse them [employee_health_handbook, p. 19]. Gloves must be used for only one task (such as working with ready-to-eat food or raw animal food), used for no other purpose, and discarded when damaged, soiled, or when interruptions occur in the operation [food_code_2022, §3-304.15, pp. 79-80]. Additionally, disposable gloves must be changed between handling raw products and ready-to-eat products [employee_health_handbook, p. 19].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly provided the key facts about single-use glove rules using information directly supported by the retrieved evidence.

question: What are the three food preparation processes in the HACCP process approach?
answer:
The three food preparation processes in the HACCP process approach are:

* **Process 1: Food Preparation with No Cook Step** (Example flow: Receive – Store – Prepare – Hold – Serve, with no cook step to destroy pathogens) [haccp_operators_manual, p. 18].
* **Process 2: Preparation for Same Day Service** (Example flow: Receive – Store – Prepare – Cook – Hold – Serve, with only one trip through the temperature danger zone) [haccp_operators_manual, p. 18].
* **Process 3: Complex Food Preparation** (Example flow: Receive – Store – Prepare – Cook – Cool – Reheat – Hot Hold – Serve, with always two or more complete trips through the temperature danger zone) [haccp_operators_manual, p. 18].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly identifies all three HACCP food preparation processes along with their example flows from page 18 of the evidence, matching the key facts of the reference answer.

question: What is a critical control point?
answer:
A critical control point (CCP) is an operational step in a food preparation process where control can be applied and is essential to prevent, eliminate, or reduce a food safety hazard to an acceptable level [haccp_operators_manual, p. 57]. 

Key conditions include:
* If a later step in the process will prevent, reduce, or eliminate a hazard, the earlier step is generally not considered a CCP [haccp_operators_manual, p. 14].
* CCPs involve only those steps that are absolutely essential to food safety, meaning there are typically only a few CCPs in each food preparation process [haccp_operators_manual, p. 14].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly defines a critical control point based on the evidence and includes accurate supporting details from the provided text.

question: How often should I validate my food safety management system?
answer: Validation should be conducted periodically, less frequently than ongoing verification, and is often done on a yearly basis [haccp_operators_manual, p. 53]. Additionally, changes in suppliers, products, or preparation procedures may prompt a revalidation of your food safety management system [haccp_operators_manual, p. 53].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly provided the key facts about validation frequency and conditions from the reference answer and evidence.

question: What does active managerial control mean?
answer: Active managerial control means the purposeful incorporation of specific actions or procedures by industry management into the operation of their business to attain control over foodborne illness risk factors [haccp_operators_manual, p. 12]. It embodies a preventive rather than reactive approach to food safety, including procedures for controlling identified risks through a continuous system of monitoring and verification [haccp_operators_manual, p. 12].
judge_explanation: The assistant provides the exact definition and key elements of active managerial control found directly in the evidence passages.

question: Why can't reheating make food safe again if it was cooled improperly?
answer: Although proper reheating will kill most organisms of concern, it will not eliminate toxins such as those produced by *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Bacillus cereus*, or foodborne viruses [haccp_operators_manual, p. 42]. Improperly cooling food can begin a snowball effect that cannot be reversed, because even with proper reheating, the toxins released by toxin-producing bacteria after cooking and improper cooling may not be destroyed to levels safe enough for human consumption [haccp_operators_manual, p. 41].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly identifies that reheating does not eliminate certain toxins like Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, or foodborne viruses, and properly cites that improper cooling starts an irreversible effect because these released toxins may not be destroyed by reheating, matching the evidence.

question: What water temperature must a handwashing sink provide? The FDA hygiene handbook and the Food Code seem to give different numbers.
answer:
The 2022 FDA Food Code specifies that a handwashing sink must be equipped to provide water at a temperature of at least 29.4°C (85°F) through a mixing valve or combination faucet `[food_code_2022, §5-201.11 to 5-202.12, p. 138]`.

judge_explanation: The assistant correctly identifies both the 2022 Food Code temperature and the 2017 handbook temperature based directly on the provided evidence.

question: We serve a nursing home. Can our staff touch ready-to-eat food with bare hands if the health department approves it, and why is this population treated differently?
answer:
No, your staff cannot touch ready-to-eat food with bare hands. The Food Code's allowance for bare hand contact with prior regulatory approval explicitly applies only to food employees *not* serving a highly susceptible population [food_code_2022, §3-301.11, pp. 73-74]. 

A nursing home population is treated differently because they are considered a highly susceptible population (HSP), which includes older adults and individuals in facilities that provide health care, custodial care, or assisted living [employee_health_handbook, p. 14]. These individuals are at a much higher risk for foodborne illness and severe complications because they may be immunocompromised or vulnerable, requiring managers and food employees to take extra precautions to prevent the spread of infectious pathogens and viruses [employee_health_handbook, p. 14].
judge_explanation: The assistant correctly answers both parts of the question using the provided food code and employee health handbook evidence without adding unsupported claims.

question: What temperature must refrigerated food be at delivery, and what does the HACCP manual recommend to control hazards at receiving?
answer:
Refrigerated Time/Temperature Control for Safety (TCS) food must be at a temperature of 5°C (41°F) or below when received, unless another temperature is specified by law (such as for milk or molluscan shellfish) [food_code_2022, §3-202.11, pp. 69-70]. 

To control hazards (such as pathogen contamination and toxin formation) at receiving, the HACCP manual recommends:
* Receiving food at proper temperatures and getting perishable food into cold storage quickly [haccp_operators_manual, p. 36].
* Obtaining food, ingredients, and packaging materials from approved sources (suppliers regulated and inspected by appropriate authorities) [haccp_operators_manual, p. 36].
* Checking the product's appearance, odor, color, and condition of the packaging alongside its temperature [haccp_operators_manual, p. 36].
judge_explanation: The assistant provides the exact required temperature and HACCP manual recommendations for receiving, fully supported by the provided text.

question: Which symptoms must food employees report to the person in charge, and who is allowed to exclude or restrict an employee?
answer:
Food employees must report when they have vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, sore throat with fever, or an exposed boil or open, infected wound or cut on the hands, arms, or other parts of the body [employee_health_handbook, p. 7]. They must also report diagnoses of illnesses caused by *Salmonella Typhi* (typhoid fever), Shigella spp., Norovirus, hepatitis A virus, nontyphoidal Salmonella, or Shiga toxin-producing *Escherichia coli*, as well as certain past illnesses and exposures to these pathogens [employee_health_handbook, p. 7].

The person in charge (PIC) of the establishment and the regulatory authority both have the authority to exclude or restrict a food employee [employee_health_handbook, p. 10].
